analysis.one_liner: Phases out the separate lower minimum wage for tipped workers and guarantees they keep their tips.
analysis.headline: Introduced September 3, 2025 with 13 Democratic cosponsors and referred to two House committees; neither committee has held a hearing or scheduled a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage for tipped workers — now just $2.13 an hour in states that allow a 'tip credit' — to $3.60 in the first year and by $1.50 each year after, until it reaches the regular federal minimum wage. It would also bar employers from keeping any of their workers' tips, stop managers from taking a share, and stop tips from being used to pay credit-card processing fees. Finally, it would let workers vote to create or change tip pools and force employers to disclose what happens to mandatory service charges.
analysis.who_benefits: Tipped workers in states where employers can pay as little as $2.13 an hour and count customers' tips toward the minimum. They would see their guaranteed cash wage rise every year until it matched the regular federal minimum, and they would keep every tip they receive, with managers, supervisors, and card fees unable to take a cut. Workers would also gain the right to vote on whether tip pooling exists and how it works.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the separate tipped minimum wage: tipped employees would have to be paid the wage in the regular federal minimum wage provision, with a transition that pays $3.60 an hour in the first year and adds $1.50 each year after until the regular minimum is reached [S2].

Bars employers from keeping or using employees' tips for any purpose, and spells out that letting managers or supervisors keep tips and using tips to cover credit or debit card transaction fees are violations [S2].

Gives workers a vote on tip pooling: if 30% of nonsupervisory employees request it, a pool can be created or changed when 51% of them vote yes, and pools must be voluntary, exclude anyone with hiring, firing, or scheduling authority, and keep funds in separate accounts [S2].

Treats mandatory charges that customers could reasonably believe go to workers as tips, and requires employers to disclose the reason for such charges and promptly pay over any portion promised to employees [S2].
Expands civil penalties so violations of any tip protection provision — not just tip-credit violations — carry the same penalty, covering tips unlawfully 'used or kept' [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Full-service restaurants and other employers of tipped workers, who would face a cash wage rising from $2.13 toward the full federal minimum over several years, plus the cost of administering tip-pool votes and records and of absorbing card processing fees they can no longer deduct from tips.

drawbacks.text: The end point is only the regular federal minimum wage, which has been $7.25 an hour since 2009 — the bill equalizes tipped workers up to that low floor rather than to a higher wage [S2].
The transition keeps a subminimum wage in place for several years: $3.60 an hour in the first year, still well below the $7.25 federal minimum [S2].

In tip-pool disputes the employer may mediate and impose a resolution on participating employees, though only after majorities of both service and back-of-house employees fail to agree, and the bill requires employees to prove a 30% request and a 51% vote before a pool can be changed [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For tipped workers in the many states still using the $2.13 tip credit, this is a substantial, multi-year raise and the strongest tip-retention protections yet written into federal law. The costs fall on restaurant and tipped-service employers, who would likely raise menu prices or adjust staffing to cover the higher cash wage, and some high-tipping servers could see tip income soften if tipping norms shift. The bill's main design weakness is that its end point is the stale $7.25 federal minimum, so in states that already pay tipped workers the full minimum it changes little — its value is concentrated in low-tip-wage states, and it would take several years to get there.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in September 2025 and sent to two House committees, Education and Workforce and Ways and Means, and neither committee has taken it up; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Jahana Hayes introduced the Tipped Worker Protection Act on September 3, 2025, with 11 original cosponsors [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the Education and Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction; the action history shows no further steps [S4].
Thirteen House Democrats had signed on as cosponsors, with no Republican cosponsors listed [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, tipped-service employers: in states that allow it, they can still pay a $2.13 hourly cash wage and count tips toward the minimum, because the bill has not advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors are House Democrats and no Republican has signed on; Republicans hold a 223–217 House majority, and the committees where the bill sits are chaired by the majority party.

industries.industry: Full-service restaurants and other tipped-service employers
industries.note: The bill raises the cash wage these employers must pay from $2.13 toward the full federal minimum, ends their ability to count tips toward the wage, and stops them from paying card transaction fees out of tips. Their cost is the worker raise the bill delivers, so in this bill their interest runs directly against tipped workers'.

The bill does not touch the fees themselves, but it bars employers from covering those fees with employees' tips, so the pass-through to workers ends and the cost shifts to the employer side of the transaction.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding a 223–217 House majority, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action in the months since referral, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing. Like most minimum wage bills from the minority party, it will most likely sit in committee until this Congress ends in January 2027.
